title: Saragarhi, 1897
hook: twenty-one Sikh soldiers hold a signal post against thousands on the frontier

segments.voice: Yesterday, Singh Sabha, and your line, renewal begins at school. Did you teach or learn one small thing? Today, twenty-one men at a lonely hilltop post. Day two hundred ninety-six.

Some jobs look small until the moment they aren't. The lifeguard who watches an empty pool all summer. The night nurse checking the same monitors. The person who keeps a signal lamp lit on a hill so two forts can talk to each other. Nobody writes songs about the quiet days. But on a September morning in 1897, on a ridge in the mountains of the northwest frontier, the quiet job became the whole world for twenty-one men. Today: Saragarhi.
screen: `JOBS THAT LOOK SMALL.` → `A SIGNAL POST BETWEEN TWO FORTS.` → `SEPTEMBER, 1897.`

segments.voice: Garhi means a small fort. Saragarhi was a little stone post on the Samana ridge, in the mountains of what is now northwest Pakistan. Its job was to pass signals by heliograph, flashes of sunlight from a mirror, between two larger British forts that couldn't see each other. It was held by twenty-one soldiers of a Sikh regiment of the British Indian Army, the 36th Sikhs, under Havildar Ishar Singh. The region was in revolt; the local Pashtun tribes were fighting to keep the British out of their valleys. On the twelfth of September, several thousand tribal fighters surrounded the post. Popular retellings say they were offered safe passage if they gave up the post. They stayed. They held for hours, against far greater numbers. One of them, the signaler Gurmukh Singh, kept flashing messages to the fort, reporting the fight as it happened, until the very end. Then, the story goes, he asked permission to leave his post, picked up his rifle, and fought until he fell. All twenty-one died. Each was given the highest gallantry award then open to Indian soldiers. Sikhs, and the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army today, remember the twelfth of September as Saragarhi Day. Sikhs often tell it alongside the old stories of the Khalsa: saint-soldiers who stood their ground. It's worth remembering too that the men on the other side were fighting for their own homes. The lesson Sikhs draw isn't about them. It's about twenty-one people who stayed at a small post when staying mattered.
screen: `GARHI — A SMALL FORT.` · `A SIGNAL POST ON THE SAMANA RIDGE.` · `TWENTY-ONE AGAINST THOUSANDS.` · `THE SIGNALER KEPT SIGNALING.` · then, large: `TWENTY-ONE HELD.`

segments.voice: Think of one small duty in your life that others quietly depend on. Taking out the bins. Picking up a child. Answering the email that keeps a project moving. Showing up on time for a shift. Picture the people who'd feel it if you let it slide. Now decide to hold that post today, fully, without cutting corners. Nobody needs to notice. Rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Saragarhi. The small signal post where, in 1897, twenty-one Sikh soldiers held against thousands, and the signaler kept signaling until the end.
Your line: twenty-one held. Today, stand firm in one small duty that others depend on. Day two hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs and the Sikh Regiment of the Indian Army mark Saragarhi Day each year on 12 September; memorial gurdwaras for the twenty-one stand in Amritsar and Ferozepur.

fork.setup: you're one of twenty-one at a small signal post. thousands are coming. you're offered safe passage if you give up the post. what do you do?
fork.reveal: the twenty-one stayed and held for hours. all of them died at their post.

original.note: Gurmukhi: garhi, a small fort, as in Saragarhi and Chamkaur di Garhi.

trapdoor: what you thought: a famous last stand.
what it means: twenty-one soldiers who chose to stay at a small post that others depended on, and held it to the end.

what a scholar hears: 12 September 1897, Tirah campaign; 36th Sikhs (now 4th Battalion, the Sikh Regiment); all twenty-one received the Indian Order of Merit posthumously; attackers were Orakzai and Afridi tribesmen, numbers estimated in the thousands.

sources.ref: The defense of Saragarhi, 12 September 1897, as recorded in military history

notes: Whether the defenders were explicitly offered the chance to leave is found in popular accounts; confirm or soften.
Gurmukh Singh asking permission to leave his post and take up his rifle is part of the traditional account; framed as 'the story goes'.
Numbers of attackers vary widely (often 8,000–10,000); kept as 'several thousand'.
The script notes the attackers were defending their own valleys, to avoid demonizing them; Keeper to confirm the framing, since this was a British colonial campaign.

Review (fresh editor): the claim that the defenders were 'told they could leave' and stayed 'so the fort beyond would have time' is not in the regimental record; now framed as what popular retellings say (an offer of safe passage), with the myth and fork adjusted to match. 'Impossible numbers' softened.
